claims.text: Controlled rapid solidification followed by tailored thermal cycling can induce an fcc matrix containing a minor hcp phase in a high-entropy alloy.
The resulting fcc+hcp microstructure will synergistically improve strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventionally processed single-phase alloys.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi made by conventional casting or selective laser melting has a predominantly fcc initial structure.
Rapid solidification will refine the alloy microstructure.
A controlled subcritical annealing or thermal cycle can nucleate and stabilize a minor hcp phase in an fcc matrix.
Partial fcc-to-hcp transformation can occur through stacking-fault formation and transformation-induced plasticity.
Excessive treatment temperature or duration can drive complete transformation to hcp or another brittle phase.
The proposed method requires a moderate fcc-to-hcp transformation barrier.
The treatment will produce finely dispersed nanoscale hcp regions at grain or sub-grain boundaries within a predominantly fcc matrix.
The dual-phase microstructure promotes transformation-induced plasticity.
The fcc and hcp phases promote load partitioning.
Nanoscale hcp domains impede dislocation motion.
Nanoscale hcp domains provide sites for mechanical-energy dissipation.
The dislocation barriers and energy-dissipation sites increase strength while enhancing ductility and fracture resistance.
Interfaces between the fcc and hcp phases can increase the apparent Young's modulus through improved lattice integrity and load sharing.
The treated alloy will have approximately 15–20% greater yield strength than the single-phase baseline.
The treated alloy will have approximately 15–20% greater fracture resistance than the single-phase baseline.
The treatment will maintain or slightly enhance ductility.
The treatment will maintain or modestly increase Young's modulus.
An excessive hcp phase fraction can cause embrittlement and eliminate the proposed synergistic improvement.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome assigns the 15–20% target only to yield strength and fracture resistance while allowing merely maintained ductility and comparable modulus, but the falsification rule ambiguously applies a roughly 15% enhancement criterion to the combined performance of all four properties.
